units.title: Hello, Elixir
units.summary: Write your first Elixir script, print text with IO.puts, join strings and add comments.

lesson.md: Elixir is a friendly language for building reliable programs. You write a program in a **script** file that ends in `.exs`, for example `hello.exs`. In a terminal, the command `elixir hello.exs` runs it.

lesson.code: IO.puts("Hello, Elixir!")

lesson.md: `IO.puts` prints text and then starts a new line. `IO` is a **module** (a group of functions) and `puts` is a function inside it. The dot `.` connects the module and the function. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello, Elixir!"`, is a **string**.

lesson.code:
IO.puts("Line one")
IO.puts("Line two")
IO.puts(2 + 3)

lesson.md: The program runs from top to bottom, one line after the other. `IO.puts` can also print numbers and the result of a calculation, like `2 + 3`.
The operator `<>` joins two strings into one. With `=` you give a value a name: `name = "Ada"`. Later you write `name` to use the value. Such a name is called a **variable**.

lesson.code:
name = "Ada"
IO.puts("Hello, " <> name)
IO.puts("Bye, " <> name <> "!")

lesson.md: `IO.inspect` shows a value the way Elixir writes it in code. A string appears with its quotes, so you can see what kind of value it is. This helps a lot when you look for mistakes.

lesson.code:
IO.puts("hi")
IO.inspect("hi")
IO.inspect(42)

lesson.md: A line that starts with `#` is a **comment**. Elixir ignores it. You can use `#` to switch off a line of code without deleting it.

lesson.code:
IO.puts("one")
# IO.puts("two")
IO.puts("three")

lesson.md: You can leave out the parentheses: `IO.puts "Hi"` works too. In this course you always write them, because it makes the code easier to read.

card: `IO.puts("Hi")` prints text and a new line

units.title: Basic types
units.summary: Work with integers, floats, atoms, booleans and strings, and put values into strings with interpolation.

lesson.md: Elixir has two kinds of numbers. An **integer** is a whole number like `7`. A **float** is a number with a decimal point like `3.5`. You calculate with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`.

lesson.code:
IO.puts(7 + 3)
IO.puts(7 * 3)
IO.puts(10 / 2)
IO.puts(7 / 2)

lesson.md: The operator `/` always gives a float, even when the result is whole: `10 / 2` is `5.0`. For whole-number division use `div(a, b)`. `rem(a, b)` gives the rest (the **remainder**) of that division.

lesson.code:
IO.puts(div(17, 5))
IO.puts(rem(17, 5))

lesson.md: An **atom** is a name that stands for itself. It starts with a colon, like `:ok` or `:error`. The **booleans** `true` and `false` are the answers to questions like `5 > 3`. You compare with `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`, and you combine with `and`, `or` and `not`. Functions like `is_integer` and `is_float` check the type of a value.

lesson.code:
IO.inspect(:ok)
IO.inspect(5 > 3)
IO.inspect(2 != 2)
IO.inspect(true and not false)
IO.inspect(is_integer(4))
IO.inspect(is_float(4))

lesson.md: Inside a string, `#{...}` puts a value into the text. This is called **interpolation**. Between the braces you can write any expression, for example `age + 1`.

lesson.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
IO.puts("#{name} is #{age} years old.")
IO.puts("Next year: #{age + 1}")
lesson.output:
Ada is 36 years old.
Next year: 37

lesson.md: The module `String` has many functions for text. `String.length` counts the characters and `String.upcase` turns all letters into capitals.

lesson.code:
word = "elixir"
IO.puts(String.length(word))
IO.puts(String.upcase(word))

lesson.md: `String.upcase(word)` returns a new string. The value of `word` does not change. In Elixir, values never change; you always create new ones.

units.title: Pattern matching
units.summary: Use the match operator to unpack tuples and lists, ignore values and keep values with the pin operator.

lesson.md: In Elixir, `=` is the **match operator**. Elixir makes the left side match the right side. When the left side is a variable, the variable gets the value. Because it is a match, `5 = x` is also valid when `x` is 5. When the two sides do not match, the program stops with a `MatchError`.

lesson.code:
x = 5
IO.puts(x)
5 = x
IO.puts("5 matches x")

lesson.md: A **tuple** groups a fixed number of values in curly braces: `{"Ada", 36}`. With a match you take a tuple apart and give each part a name.
Many functions return tuples like `{:ok, value}` or `{:error, reason}`. An atom in a pattern must be exactly equal, so `{:ok, result}` only matches a tuple that starts with `:ok`.

lesson.code:
{:ok, result} = {:ok, 42}
IO.puts(result)

lesson.md: A **list** holds values in square brackets: `[10, 20, 30]`. A list pattern matches only a list with the same number of items. The underscore `_` matches any value and ignores it.

lesson.code:
[a, b, c] = [10, 20, 30]
IO.puts(a + b + c)
{_, count} = {:apples, 7}
IO.puts(count)

lesson.md: You can match a variable again: `x = 2` gives `x` a new value. If you want to use the current value of `x` instead, put the **pin operator** `^` in front of it. Then `^x = 2` only checks that the value is 2.

lesson.code:
x = 1
IO.puts(x)
x = 2
IO.puts(x)
^x = 2
IO.puts("still #{x}")

lesson.md: A pinned variable never gets a new value. If `x` is 2, then `^x = 3` raises a `MatchError`.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program choose with if and else, case, cond and guards with when.

lesson.md: `if` runs code only when a condition is true. The code goes between `do` and `end`. The part after `else` runs when the condition is not true. Only `false` and `nil` (which means "no value") count as false; every other value counts as true, also `0` and `""`.

lesson.code:
temp = 25

if temp > 20 do
  IO.puts("warm")
else
  IO.puts("cold")
end

lesson.md: `if` returns a value, so you can store its result in a variable. For short cases there is a one-line form with `do:` and `else:`. Note the commas.

lesson.code:
age = 15
label = if age >= 18, do: "adult", else: "minor"
IO.puts(label)

lesson.md: `case` compares a value with several **patterns**, from top to bottom. The first pattern that matches wins, and the code after its arrow `->` runs. Variables in the pattern get their values from the match.

lesson.code:
result = {:ok, 7}

case result do
  {:ok, n} -> IO.puts("got #{n}")
  {:error, msg} -> IO.puts("error: #{msg}")
end

lesson.md: `cond` checks several conditions from top to bottom and runs the code of the first one that is true. The last condition is often `true`, which always matches. It works like a final `else`.

lesson.code:
score = 72

cond do
  score >= 90 -> IO.puts("A")
  score >= 70 -> IO.puts("B")
  true -> IO.puts("C")
end

lesson.md: A **guard** adds a condition to a pattern with the keyword `when`. The pattern matches only when the guard is also true. The pattern `_` at the end catches every other value.

lesson.code:
n = -4

case n do
  x when x < 0 -> IO.puts("negative")
  0 -> IO.puts("zero")
  _ -> IO.puts("positive")
end

lesson.md: If no pattern of a `case` matches, the program stops with a `CaseClauseError`. If no condition of a `cond` is true, it stops with a `CondClauseError`. Add `_ ->` or `true ->` at the end to avoid this.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:

else

exercises.explain: `rem(7, 2)` is 1, so the condition is false and the `else` part runs.

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write anonymous functions, named functions in modules, and chain calls with the pipe operator.

lesson.md: A function takes values (its **arguments**) and returns a result. `fn x -> x * 2 end` is an **anonymous function**: it has no name, but you can store it in a variable. To call it, write a dot before the parentheses: `double.(4)`.

lesson.code:
double = fn x -> x * 2 end
IO.puts(double.(4))

lesson.md: Arguments are separated by commas. The function returns the value of its last expression; Elixir has no `return` keyword.

lesson.code:
add = fn a, b -> a + b end
IO.puts(add.(2, 3))

lesson.md: Named functions live in a **module**. `defmodule` creates the module and `def` defines a function inside it. Module names start with a capital letter. You call the function with the module name and a dot, without an extra dot before the parentheses: `Math.square(5)`.

lesson.code:
defmodule Math do
  def square(n) do
    n * n
  end
end

IO.puts(Math.square(5))

lesson.md: A short function fits on one line with `, do:`. A function can have several **clauses** with different patterns. Elixir tries them from top to bottom and runs the first one that matches. Guards with `when` work here too.

lesson.code:
defmodule Greeter do
  def hello(:es), do: "Hola"
  def hello(:fr), do: "Bonjour"
  def hello(_), do: "Hello"
end

IO.puts(Greeter.hello(:fr))
IO.puts(Greeter.hello(:de))

defmodule Check do
  def sign(n) when n < 0, do: "negative"
  def sign(0), do: "zero"
  def sign(_), do: "positive"
end

IO.puts(Check.sign(-3))
IO.puts(Check.sign(0))

lesson.md: A function is known by its name and its number of arguments, the **arity**. You write it as `square/1` or `add/2`. `defp` instead of `def` makes a **private** function that only the same module can call.

The **pipe operator** `|>` takes the result on its left and passes it as the first argument to the function on its right. `"hi" |> String.upcase()` is the same as `String.upcase("hi")`. A chain of pipes reads from top to bottom.

lesson.code:
"elixir"
|> String.upcase()
|> String.reverse()
|> IO.puts()

card: Clauses are tried from top to bottom

units.title: Lists and maps
units.summary: Store many values in lists and maps, split lists into head and tail, and use keyword lists and Map functions.

lesson.md: A list keeps values in order. `++` joins two lists, `--` removes items, and `length` counts the items. To print a list, use `IO.inspect`; `IO.puts` is only for text and numbers.

lesson.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
IO.inspect(nums ++ [4, 5])
IO.inspect([1, 2, 3, 2] -- [2])
IO.puts(length(nums))

lesson.md: The pattern `[head | tail]` splits a list. `head` gets the first item and `tail` gets a list with all the other items. The same `|` also adds an item to the front: `[5 | tail]`. The tail of a one-item list is the empty list `[]`, and `[]` itself does not match `[head | tail]`.

lesson.code:
[head | tail] = [10, 20, 30]
IO.inspect(head)
IO.inspect(tail)
IO.inspect([5 | tail])

lesson.md: A **map** stores values under **keys**: `%{name: "Ada", age: 36}`. When the keys are atoms, you read a value with `user.name` or `user[:name]`. For a missing key, `user[:email]` gives `nil`, while `user.email` stops with a `KeyError`.

lesson.code:
user = %{name: "Ada", age: 36}
IO.puts(user.name)
IO.puts(user[:age])
IO.inspect(user[:email])

lesson.md: You can match maps too. A map pattern only needs the keys it names, so `%{name: name} = user` takes the name out of `user`, even though `user` also has the key `:age`.

`Map.put` returns a new map with one more key; the old map does not change. `Map.get(map, key, default)` returns the default when the key is missing. `%{map | key: value}` returns a copy with a new value for a key that already exists.

lesson.code:
prices = %{apple: 2, pear: 3}
more = Map.put(prices, :plum, 5)
IO.inspect(more)
IO.inspect(prices)
IO.puts(Map.get(prices, :kiwi, 0))
IO.inspect(%{prices | apple: 4})

lesson.md: A **keyword list** is a list of pairs with atom keys, written `[size: 10, color: "red"]`. It is a short way to write `[{:size, 10}, {:color, "red"}]`. Functions often take options in this form. You read a value with `opts[:color]`.

lesson.code:
opts = [size: 10, color: "red"]
IO.puts(opts[:color])
IO.inspect(opts == [{:size, 10}, {:color, "red"}])

units.title: Enum and ranges
units.summary: Transform lists and ranges with Enum.map, filter, reduce and sum, and write short functions with the capture operator.

lesson.md: The module `Enum` has functions that work with every item of a list. `Enum.map(list, function)` calls the function for each item and returns a new list with the results.

lesson.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
IO.inspect(Enum.map(nums, fn n -> n * 10 end))

lesson.md: `Enum.filter` keeps only the items for which the function returns `true`. `Enum.sum` adds all items, `Enum.max` finds the largest one and `Enum.count` counts them.

lesson.code:
nums = [4, 7, 10, 13]
IO.inspect(Enum.filter(nums, fn n -> rem(n, 2) == 0 end))
IO.puts(Enum.sum(nums))
IO.puts(Enum.max(nums))

lesson.md: A **range** like `1..5` stands for all whole numbers from 1 to 5, including both ends. `Enum` functions work with ranges too. `Enum.to_list` turns a range into a list.

lesson.code:
IO.inspect(Enum.to_list(1..5))
IO.puts(Enum.sum(1..100))

lesson.md: `Enum.reduce(list, start, function)` combines all items into one value. The function gets an item and the **accumulator** `acc`, the result so far. It returns the new result. `acc` starts with the value `start`.

lesson.code:
product = Enum.reduce(1..5, 1, fn n, acc -> n * acc end)
IO.puts(product)

lesson.md: The **capture operator** `&` writes short functions. In `&(&1 * 2)`, `&1` is the first argument, so it means `fn x -> x * 2 end`. `&String.upcase/1` turns the named function `String.upcase` with arity 1 into a function value.

lesson.code:
IO.inspect(Enum.map([1, 2, 3], &(&1 * 2)))
IO.inspect(Enum.map(["a", "b"], &String.upcase/1))

lesson.md: `Enum` functions take the list as their first argument, so they work well with the pipe. This pipeline keeps the even numbers from 1 to 10, squares them and adds them up.

lesson.code:
1..10
|> Enum.filter(&(rem(&1, 2) == 0))
|> Enum.map(&(&1 * &1))
|> Enum.sum()
|> IO.puts()

card: `Enum.reduce(list, 0, fn x, acc -> x + acc end)`

units.title: Recursion
units.summary: Repeat work with functions that call themselves, stop them with a base case, and carry results in an accumulator.

lesson.md: Elixir has no `while` loop. To repeat work, a function calls itself. This is called **recursion**. Every recursive function needs a **base case**: a clause that stops without calling itself again.

lesson.code:
defmodule Count do
  def down(0), do: IO.puts("Go!")

  def down(n) do
    IO.puts(n)
    down(n - 1)
  end
end

Count.down(3)

lesson.md: `down(3)` prints 3 and calls `down(2)`, which prints 2 and calls `down(1)`, and so on. `down(0)` matches the first clause, the base case, so the calls stop there.
With `[head | tail]` a function handles the first item and leaves the rest of the list to a recursive call. The base case is the empty list `[]`.

lesson.code:
defmodule MyList do
  def sum([]), do: 0
  def sum([head | tail]), do: head + sum(tail)
end

IO.puts(MyList.sum([4, 5, 6]))

lesson.md: Step by step: `sum([4, 5, 6])` is `4 + sum([5, 6])`, which is `4 + 5 + sum([6])`, which is `4 + 5 + 6 + sum([])`. `sum([])` is 0, so the result is 15.
A recursive function can also build a new list. Here each call puts the doubled head in front of the result for the tail.

lesson.code:
defmodule Double do
  def all([]), do: []
  def all([h | t]), do: [h * 2 | all(t)]
end

IO.inspect(Double.all([1, 2, 3]))

lesson.md: An **accumulator** is an extra argument that carries the result so far. A public function starts it with a first value and a private helper made with `defp` does the work. When the list is empty, the helper returns the accumulator.

lesson.code:
defmodule Counter do
  def count(list), do: count(list, 0)

  defp count([], acc), do: acc
  defp count([_ | tail], acc), do: count(tail, acc + 1)
end

IO.puts(Counter.count([:a, :b, :c]))

lesson.md: Put the base case before the general clause, and make sure each call gets closer to it. Without a base case that matches, the function never stops.
In real programs, `Enum.sum`, `Enum.map` and `Enum.count` do this work for you. Inside, they use the same idea: recursion.

exercises.explain: The base case stops the recursion. Without it, the function would call itself forever.

IO.puts(M.biggest([4, 9, 2]))
